en: Master Ji composed this treatise. However, the meaning of "seeds" (bīja) briefly comprises six types. The commentary states:
Within the ten meanings extensively explained among the seeds, from here below is the eighth [section], which possesses many meanings. These seeds have six characteristics that exclude all others.
Among these, there are three parts.
First, the six meanings are presented in general.
Next follows the detailed explanation according to six categories.
Finally, there is a summary that distinguishes other factors as not being actual seeds.
This is the first [section].
The fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that there are seven seeds;

since this [text] mentions six, it is said to be an abbreviated account. Among the five aggregates of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), the first excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the third excludes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
This constitutes the complete differentiation.
However, regarding the further establishment of other categories for the specific locus of "self-exclusion" (*sva-sthāna-vyavaccheda*),
and the subsequent non-elaboration of the second category, "exclusion of others" (*anya-vyavaccheda*), and so forth, they shall not be recounted here.
As for the statement that "it does not exclude matter" (*rūpa*):
this is because external seeds of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) also possess these six characteristics.
[Therefore,] they are merely designated as "seeds. If that is so, how can they exist simultaneously with their fruit?
Furthermore, how can it be said that [the seeds] "constantly and perpetually evolve"? In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, no distinction is made; it simply states that internal seeds exist.
Vasubandhu provides the explanation for this, yet each of those points is explained by him individually.
It is said that while internal phenomena are thus and external phenomena are thus,
when it comes to the simultaneous presence [of the fruit], one speaks only of internal seeds,
without mentioning external ones.
Examine each of these in turn to clarify them.
Now, it will be explained that external seeds also possess fruits that coexist with them,
such as the lotus root producing the lotus flower and so forth.
It is not the case that the fruit arises only at the moment the cause ceases,
for it is universally established in the world that roots and stems exist simultaneously;
this interpretation is somewhat better.
One should investigate this in detail. According to the treatise,
it must perish in a single moment before it can become a seed.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the meaning of "seed," which refers to the fact that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess arising and ceasing.
In the state of transformation, that which possesses the superior capacity to grasp and yield its fruit is what constitutes a seed.
— Treatise.
This negates the permanent dharma reaching its capacity for production.
The commentary states:
This is a concise summary.
The unconditioned is not so,
because it is devoid of transformation;
it lacks the functions of grasping and bestowing, and thus cannot be a producer.

This also clarifies that for the four schools of the Mahāsāṃghika and others, as well as the Mahīśāsaka school, dependent origination is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it is without appropriation (*anupādāna*) and without relinquishment (*anapavāda*), and is devoid of transformation (*avikāra*).
This immediately refutes the Vaibhāṣika masters' doctrine of the four characteristics over a long duration,
because [things] do not perish instantaneously. If it is argued that there is superior functional capacity at a later time,
whereas it was absent in the initial stage:
It should also exist at the beginning,
because its substance is one,
just as it does at a later time; yet it should not exist at the end.
Because its substance is one,
as in the preceding state,
it is called a "seed" because it perishes immediately upon the very moment its substance arises.
It possesses superior causal power;

it exists as soon as it arises and does not depend on a later time. Furthermore, it excludes the eternal principles such as *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and the *ātman* asserted by non-Buddhists as causes, because these lack the capacity for transformation.
The fifth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Only impermanent phenomena serve as causes;
permanent phenomena do not. Those of the old school claim that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the seed of all phenomena.
No. If that were so, then a preceding seed would have to serve as the seed for a subsequent moment’s manifest activity;
or else, even within the same moment, seeds would have to exist in relation to one another across different bodies.
[Treatise]
"The two fruits must both be present before it can be established as a seed.
The commentary states:
This means that this seed must await the fruit-dharmas of actual manifestation that are to be produced [before it can be called a seed].
"Existing simultaneously. Regarding "existing," there are three senses in which it is called "existing": manifestation, the present, and being manifest.
For this reason, in those who lack such natures, the seventh consciousness is not termed a "seed."
Because the fruit does not manifest,
the term "manifesting" excludes that seventh [consciousness].
"Present" excludes what precedes and follows it.
There currently exist provisional phenomena;
their substance is substantially established because they possess seeds,
and they manifest exclusively as fruits.
That which exists presently exists only as a cause.
The present [dharma] is common to both cause and effect; it is "conjoined" (sāmagrī) and distinguished from being "separated" (visamyukta).
This specifically excludes a preceding dharma from being the seed of a subsequent dharma.
Some say that when seeds give rise to manifest activity,
it necessarily occurs across preceding and succeeding moments, rather than within this single moment.
How is this to be understood?
That master’s intention is to say that,
according to the Sthavira school, the mind exists at two distinct times.
Since the cause exists while the effect is in the process of arising, they both coexist in the present;
thus, there is no contradiction.
This is the position elucidated by the Venerable Upāśānta (Shengjun).
This is not practical;
it shall be explained in detail within the third fascicle itself. If that were so, the same would apply to seeds looking toward seeds.
What, then, is the purpose of this distinction? The *Yogācārabhūmi* says:
Dharmas take their own nature (*svabhāva*) as their cause;

they do not exist at that very same moment. This [cause] must necessarily exist at a different time and is not co-existent with its effect. Even if the cause is in the state of ceasing and the effect is in the state of arising, it is still termed "co-existent."
This would entail the difficulty of two destinies arising simultaneously.
From this, it is known that when a seed produces its result, they must necessarily belong to the same time period (*adhvan*).
The seeds that produce [results] do not necessarily belong to the same world-period as those [results].
Even if they must belong to the same world-period,
they only constitute seeds when they are in a state of conjunction with active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
The treatise states: "A simple [condition] cannot serve as a cause for the present activity of another body, because they are not conjoined."
This excludes [the views] of anteriority, posteriority, and fixed separation.
The commentary states:
This refutes the Sautrāntikas and others who hold that cause and effect exist at different times.
The same applies to the Theravāda and other schools:
seeds are necessarily co-existent with their manifest activity;
because they are inseparable within a single continuum, they can function as causes.
The non-Buddhists claim that Maheśvara gives birth to all sentient beings;
however, their arguments regarding the causes and conditions of sentient beings are entirely untenable.
Question: Why is it that when seeds are considered in relation to seeds as cause and effect,
they are said to arise at different times,
whereas when they are considered in relation to the manifest, they constitute cause and effect simultaneously?
Thus, it is permitted that [the seeds] arise simultaneously.
The treatise states:
"The present and the seeds, though of different categories, possess the capacity for productive function."
The commentary states:
Because manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*) belong to different categories, they do not contradict one another;
thus, they can coexist simultaneously within a single body.
Because it possesses the functional capacity to produce [effects].
For instance, in the case of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*),
their manifest activity is characterized by resistance.
The seed is unimpeded;
the mind, its objects of cognition, and so forth should be understood accordingly.
Because the essential natures of cause and effect are not similar, they are termed "different classes."
Because they are not mutually exclusive, they can exist simultaneously.
The treatise states:
"This is not like a seed, which necessarily cannot coexist [with its fruit]."
The commentary states:

When a seed is compared to [its own] seed, their essential natures being similar, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). Because they are mutually exclusive, they cannot coexist simultaneously within a single body.

The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) takes its own self-substance as an object simultaneously with its arising;
likewise, a seed produces its own self-substance simultaneously with its arising.
There is an interpretation which says:
The seed is cause and effect in relation to the seed;
if one allows them to be simultaneous, they are not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Although the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and [the object] are simultaneous, they stand in a relationship of cause and effect.

This would then not be subsumed under causal conditions (*pratyaya*). If that were so, the same would apply to the relationship between seeds and their manifesting counterparts; therefore, this must be further explained.
It is accepted that a seed arises simultaneously with another seed.
The substance would then be infinite,
because it is admitted that [factors] of the same kind arise simultaneously; thus,
within a single moment, there would be multiple types of arising.
There is no cause or condition for this,
because it is not admitted that a subsequent seed can again produce a fruit; thus,
the active manifestation (pravṛtti) is called "of a different kind" (vijātīya) in relation to the seed.
Although seeds are likewise perfumed,
there is no infinite regress because the subsequent seeds have not yet produced their fruits;
furthermore, within a single moment, two manifesting entities cannot coexist simultaneously.
The seeds produced [by this] cannot, by virtue of this, give rise to a manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) again;

the same should apply to seeds in relation to their own kind. Question: If that is so, how can new perfumings (*vāsanā*) arise from those that are originally present and share the same mental continuity?
Because their natures are contradictory, these do not exist simultaneously;
they are like the untainted *laukikāgradharma*,
which takes as its object the seeds that have existed since beginningless time.
It draws forth the naturally occurring seeds of its own kind that project the subsequent moment,
and further acts as a cause to produce a newly perfumed seed in the subsequent moment;
since the power of both the original and the new seeds is equal through their conditions, they arise together as a single manifestation.
Therefore, there is no fault of a seed arising from a seed of identical thought; yet this too is difficult to understand.
If a seed that already exists were to further produce a seed, then four dharmas would exist within a single moment.
That is to say: first, that which exists from the beginning;
second, that which arises from what exists;
and third, that which is perfumed by new active manifestations.
The fourth is actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).
How can it be said that these three factors interact with one another? This is now explained: it is not so.

That is to say, because a newly perfumed seed is produced with both the originally existing seed and the present activity serving as its causes and conditions, there are only three dharmas. Alternatively,
it is explained that the originally existing seed is not the cause or condition for the newly perfumed seed.
Because the manifesting active state (pravṛtti) acts as the efficient cause (hetu-pratyaya) for the perfuming,
this refers to the originally existing [seeds] in relation to the manifesting state;
the manifesting state, in turn, relates only to the newly perfumed [seeds].
Because it serves as a causal condition,
the essence of this prātimokṣa restraint does not increase by virtue of it.
Yet, it increases in function.
It resembles the precepts of meditative concentration (dhyāna-śīla) and the path (mārga-śīla).
Since both the precepts of concentration and the path are present volitions (cetanā), [they do not involve future rebirth].

Therefore, it is only that the function increases moment by moment, not the substance. This previous explanation accords with the principle that both the substance and the function of the prātimokṣa vows increase together.
Although this passage clarifies the simultaneous possession of the fruit, it is explained in terms of the manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
It may be said that the meaning of "cause" applies to the present time;
however, since it is already accepted that a seed is at a different time from [its own] seed,
if it enters the past, what would constitute the meaning of "cause"?

Although cause and effect ultimately lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Commentary states:
Regarding the cause and its fruit being simultaneous:
this refers to arising and manifesting. Regarding their not being simultaneous: [this refers to other cases].
Although they arise from their own kind,
whether simultaneously or not, they must exist in the present in order to possess causal efficacy;
this is because they possess substantial reality.
If it enters the past, it lacks causal efficacy because its substance has already ceased;
the same applies to the future.
Because the essence of that which has not yet arisen does not exist due to its dependence [on causes].
Question: Since the cause applies equally to seeds and to those possessing seeds, why is it said here that [the cause] exists simultaneously with its fruit?
Treatise:
From the production of the manifest fruit up to its coexistence with the giving of the fruit.
Commentary: [As follows].
The seeds that produce manifest activity upon arising are called "coexistent" (*sahabhū*);
they are not so called because they project their own kind as seeds. Why is this? Because they are produced by perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Because they differ in kind,
because the fruit has already manifested,
and because their characteristics are easily known, one seed does not act as a perfuming agent for another seed.
Because they are not of a different category,
because they do not manifest,
and because they are not easily known.
Since this is not stated therein, the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, fascicle 2, says:
"That which does not arise as actual manifestation is called the 'type' (*jāti*);
when it arises as actual manifestation, it is called the 'seed' (*bīja*). How then does Vijñānavādin Śaṃkarasvāmin explain that [the seed] is not identical to this very moment?

Because they maintain that cause and effect belong to the same temporal period, how then do they explain the passage concerning "that which has already arisen without a seed"? This is as they have compiled it;
for example, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56.
There is a passage in another excerpt;
furthermore, it may be consulted and explained in the fourth section below.
If the active perfuming factors, such as the evolving consciousnesses, were [to be considered seeds], they ought to be designated as seeds.

The three [factors] must persist and evolve until they finally become seeds.

That is to say, when its nature remains uniform and continuous without interruption over a long period until the path of the antidote is attained,
it is called reaching the stage of culmination.
Because each is ultimately [distinct]. The Commentary states:
This excludes the evolving consciousnesses from being non-associated [with the mind].
The commentary states:
It is denied that the seven evolving consciousnesses,
as well as dharmas such as form, can serve as seeds.
This refers only to the mind;
in reality, it also excludes form (*rūpa*). The Sautrāntika position that the six consciousnesses and so forth can maintain the seeds is likewise refuted herein.
Because the three types of sensation undergo transformation,
and because one easily becomes detached from the objects of perception.

this clarifies the meaning of a preceding seed producing a subsequent one.
This is not co-existent, because it is subsumed under the category of seeds.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not mention this. Question: Is the seventh consciousness also severed only upon reaching the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*)?
Why is it not called a "seed"? Answer: Because within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth, there is transformation;
because the objects of perception are easily abandoned;
and because transformation occurs immediately before an antidote has even been applied.
Seeds are not like that. If so, how can they be designated as seeds characterized by the exhaustion of experience (*vedanīya*) and seeds not characterized by the exhaustion of experience?
[It is because] the seeds of names and words (*nāma-vāk*), which are neutral (*avyākṛta*), produce fruits that are immeasurable and inexhaustible.
It can continue to evolve perpetually.
Since the fruits produced from seeds that are wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth are limited, how can they evolve perpetually? The answer is:
Based on the fact that the production of its fruit has a limit,
it is called "having the characteristic of being subject to exhaustion";
this does not mean that the substance of the seed has not yet obtained its antidote.

They are immediately extinguished without remainder. Furthermore, there is the perfuming of the "divisions" (*bhāga*), which is termed the "characteristic of having an end to experience" (*sopabhoga-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*).
The perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*) is termed "constantly evolving" (*nitya-anuvartana*).
These seeds produce fruits only from their own kind and constantly evolve.
That is to say, it is called a "seed" because it does not exist simultaneously with its fruit;
this lacks the single meaning of being "always present together with the fruit. If it lacked even one of these meanings, it could be termed a seed.
However, the seventh consciousness lacks the quality of "constantly evolving along [with its fruit]."
It should be called "seed"; however, this is not appropriate.
Herein, the meaning of "seed" is precisely revealed through the two principles of arising-and-ceasing and constant transformation.
The others merely provide specific refutations, as they do not constitute a direct demonstration.

Furthermore, it is taught that seeds must possess six characteristics. As for the seventh consciousness, it cannot be established as a seed. Moreover, it is said that seeds are endowed with six attributes.
This does not mean that being endowed with the six [elements] constitutes the seed; furthermore, these [six] of their own kind are also not seeds, because they do not coexist with their fruit.

Although the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states they are not seeds, it calls them "categories" (*jāti*). This indicates that as long as these of their own kind have not reached the stage of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), they do not receive the name "seed."
At the time when the fruit is produced, it may be called the seed;
however, if the production of the fruit necessarily occurs simultaneously [with the seed],
then as for its substantial nature (tattva):
The state of its own kind is also called a seed,
because it is not a manifest activity;
this merely functions spontaneously to draw forth a subsequent fruit.
If conditions are complete, the potential of the superior seed increases,
and when the capacity to produce a superior fruit arises,
it is then designated as a "seed. This absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) reveals the distinction between these two stages.
Both the fruit and the cause are termed "seeds" (*bīja*);

otherwise, they are termed "seed-types" (*bījajātīya*). Here, in reference to that which is not currently manifest (*apravṛtta*), its essence is spoken of by the general name "seed," which is likewise not contradictory.
Furthermore, this demonstrates that the seed possesses these six characteristics.
It is not said that every moment possesses all six characteristics and is therefore called a seed; rather, one must distinguish between them.
Only if it possesses all six characteristics is it termed a seed; if even one is lacking, it is not established as such.
Sentient beings who lack the nature [for liberation] constitute the seventh [category].
Because they lack [the seeds] that coexist with present results, these are not seeds. If that were so, then the seed would always continue to evolve even when the result has not yet arisen.
It should not be called a "seed"; this is how it should be explained.
When the path of counteraction arises, it means that [the seeds] are rendered incapable of manifesting in their active state (*samudācāra*) and so forth.
Just as with the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and so forth within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga),
which, existing in substance,
are only eliminated during the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
Seeds that do not produce their fruit are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because from the point when they are exhausted onward, there is no possibility for them to coexist with their fruit.
As for what is now called "coexisting with the fruit":
From the time the path of counteraction arises until the present,
that which possesses the meaning of being in simultaneous conjunction with the manifest resultant dharmas is called a "seed."
It is not necessary that this thought must be conjoined with the present [moment] to be called a seed;
otherwise, within a single realm, the seeds of all three realms would not be established,
and the meaning of the "accomplishment" of seeds would fail to hold.
Therefore, it is known that this is not stated in reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

Rather, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is revealed by means of the subsequent capacity to produce [an effect] and the sense of being simultaneous with the fruit. As for what was said by Vasubandhu—that when it does not produce a fruit, it is called a "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāgahetu*)—[it refers to this].
This is discussed in terms of the ultimate non-arising of future results,
such as the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
If [the cause] continues to function persistently, it may be designated as a "seed" (*bīja*).
It should be understood that wholesome [seeds] and so forth produce unwholesome [results] and so forth.
According to the treatise,
the four natures must be determined before they can constitute seeds.
The commentary states:
This means that, by the power of the causal force of the manifest activity at the time of prior perfuming, wholesome, unwholesome, and other [states] arise;
their functional capacities are determined and do not arise in a confused or disordered manner.
Treatise:
This refutes the position of other schools regarding the meaning of "having causes and conditions.
Commentary: [As follows].
This refutes the Sarvāstivādins and others [who claim] that wholesome dharmas and so forth serve as homogeneous causes for unwholesome, indeterminate, and other such [dharmas].
The Meaning of Dependent Origination: Now, as for dependent origination,
it distinguishes the arising of intrinsic nature and the conformity of characteristics.
Since wholesome factors and so forth do not distinguish themselves from unwholesome factors and so forth in terms of their intrinsic nature,
and since they do not accord with one another,
in what sense are they "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya)? Furthermore, the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) produces neutral results (avyākṛta-phala) from both wholesome and unwholesome natures.
The pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and others have results that are of a different nature.

It is likewise for the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which takes the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*), the immediate result (*anantara-phala*), and the virile result (*puruṣakāra-phala*) as its causes.
Furthermore, if one requires seeds that are wholesome and so forth to be the causes of what is wholesome and so forth, [then this principle holds].
Since the seeds exist eternally,
they should produce their fruits instantaneously.
[Treatise:]
The fifth [point] is that seeds are only established as such when they encounter various conditions.
The commentary states:
this means that one's own seeds must depend upon the convergence of various conditions.
The seed becomes a seed only when its capacity for the function of producing various results— such as the arising of grasping and manifest activity—
is preeminent through transformation; therefore,
the seed does not arise from its own kind as a causal condition.
It is not called a seed.
The treatise states that this refutes the non-Buddhists' claim that [the seed] produces its fruit eternally and instantaneously.
The commentary states:
This refers to the attachment of non-Buddhists who maintain that there exists a distinct dharma called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).
It does not depend on various conditions but constantly and simultaneously produces its effects;
this is precisely how the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon it,
and the same applies to their calculations regarding Mahābrahmā, time, space, and so forth.
This is likewise what is being refuted.
Herein, we shall first present one sense of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).
Treatise:
Or [it may be] a refutation of other schools' position that [dharmas] do not arise constantly and simultaneously.
The commentary states:
This refers to the doctrine of the existence of the three time periods (*traikālyavāda*).
The essence of conditions exists at all times, meaning it is never non-existent.

Now, by stating that seeds produce fruits only when depending on conditions, this [text] refutes that [opponent's] attachment. If conditions were eternally present, they should eternally produce fruits.
Since it is not admitted that seeds produce their fruits at all times, conditions are therefore constantly absent.
Question: Even if conditions were present, would the nature of the wholesome and so forth be fixed?
It should be understood that wholesome seeds such as form produce wholesome fruits such as the mind.
The treatise states:
"The sixth [characteristic] is that it becomes a seed only when it draws forth its own fruit."
The commentary states:
It is said that with respect to distinct results such as distinct matter and distinct mind,
that which individually induces them is alone designated as a "seed."
Material elements that are not themselves wholesome and so forth cannot be called seeds for the production of wholesome mental states and their fruits,
because they are dissociated [from them].
Treatise:
This negates the [claim of] non-Buddhists that [the self] reaches and produces all effects.
Commentary states:
The claim that Maheśvara acts as the cause from which all effects arise, and so forth,
is entirely based on this calculation;
[otherwise] the effects would have no distinction.
Since causes are distinct,
if effects already differ, their causes must likewise be different.
Therefore, it is not the case that a single cause produces all effects.
Treatise:
Or, [this] negates the other schools' [position] that [dharmas] mutually serve as causes and conditions.
Commentary states:

The Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that virtuous matter (*rūpa*) serves as a cause for the four aggregates (*skandha*), and that the four [aggregates] likewise serve as causes for the aggregate of matter; however, this is not correct.
A cause and its effect must conform to one another by producing only their own respective results.
Because their functional capacity is identical, they are termed "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya).
If it concerns the "dominant condition" (adhipati-pratyaya) and so forth,
then such a designation would indeed be appropriate.
How can form and so forth serve as causes for the mind?
Because they do not conform [to it] and their functional capacities differ.
It is asked: that which constantly follows and evolves is called a "seed."
Since the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the eighth consciousness is constantly and continuously present, does it also possess names and seeds?
Some say that it does, because it is called the "all-seed consciousness" (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*). If one were to argue thus:
Since this manifestation, in relation to its own seeds,
is neither a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) nor an impregnating agent (*bhāvakatva*), how can it be called a "seed"?
Some say that [the term] "all-seed consciousness" cannot be applied to it.
That which contains all phenomena (*dharma*) and is capable of producing all phenomena is called "all-seeds" (*sarvabījaka*).
It is not the case that their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) can produce its own seeds;
for although the seeds depend upon the manifest body of consciousness, [the manifestation itself does not produce them].
This consciousness is the object of perception (*ālambana*) for [other] consciousnesses, yet it is not identical to them;

therefore, the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of consciousness is not called a "seed. What meaning is lacking here? Because it does not coexist with its fruit. Even in those of the "natureless" (*agotra*) class, the seventh consciousness likewise possesses these six characteristics.
It should be called a "seed"; yet this is not so.
The treatise itself explains that it only becomes a seed when it is present and conjoined with the manifest fruit;
the characteristic of the nature of a seed is subtle and hidden.
The characteristics of the resultant dharmas produced are coarse and manifest;
therefore, they become seeds only when coexisting with the present [consciousness].
Thus, the seventh characteristic is manifest.
When the seeds that have been perfumed are established,
the fruit remains submerged and latent,
not yet conjoined with the manifest dharmas of the fruit.
It is not called a seed;
the eighth, the manifest consciousness (ālayavijñāna), is likewise so,
because it has no produced fruit.
In the eighth section above, the categories have been clarified;
from here on, the third part provides a brief summary and distinction.
Treatise:
"Only within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) do they reach the state of seeds, and not elsewhere.
The commentary states:
This excludes the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) and others from being designated by the term "seed" (bīja).
Regarding the distinct explanation within these six meanings,
it is stated that only internal seeds possess all six characteristics;
however, Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also extends this to external seeds.
Regarding this, it is explained by way of an analogy:
if external seeds of grain or barley can produce fruit,
are they called "seeds"?
Treatise:
External grains, wheat, and so forth do not constitute actual seeds. Commentary:
[This means that]...
Although that which is transformed by consciousness is conventionally designated as a "seed," it is not a real seed,
because it is a manifest phenomenon (*dharma*). As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Because there would be the faults of [actions] performed not being lost and [results] not attained,
a contradiction would arise; therefore,
external seeds take the internal as their condition.
Based on those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*),
it is further stated in a verse:
"Heaven, earth, wind, and space."
Rivers, lakes, regions, and the great ocean—all are produced from within;
their differentiation does not exist externally. Therefore, they arise from internal seeds.
External grains and the like ripen, yet they are not actual seeds. Question: Since seeds are also transformations of consciousness, they too should not be actual seeds.
Answer: This is not so. Internal seeds, having been transformed by consciousness, subsequently give rise to wheat and other such things.
Furthermore, barley and the like are transformations of consciousness;
because they are repeated transformations,
they are not seeds.
As with the sense organ of the eye and so forth;
therefore, the subsequent text states:
"The external barley and so forth are the defining essence."
A fruit is not produced from conditions that are not causes;
therefore, causes and conditions consist solely of internal seeds, not external seeds.
All of the above is contained within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
From here below, the ninth section provides a dual analysis of the production and projection of internal and external [phenomena], citing two causes.
Do these internal and external seeds both possess the essence of the two causes—production and projection?
The answer is: they do.
Why is this? The treatise states:
"The power of these seeds reaching [the result] is called the projecting cause (ākṣepahetu)."
The commentary states:
"The production of internal and external seeds that gives rise to proximate fruits and produces the actual fruit is called the 'productive cause' (*janana-hetu*).
That which draws forth distant fruits and draws forth residual fruits is called the 'projecting cause' (*ākṣepa-hetu*). As Vasubandhu says:
For example, when internal consciousness-seeds give rise to manifest consciousnesses and so forth, these are called proximate fruits;
as causes of production,
they are distant fruits in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
This is the drawing-in cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
External seeds, in relation to the sprout, are the proximate fruit;
they are the producing cause (*janana-hetu*).
The stalk and so forth are distant fruits;
these are the projecting causes (*ākṣepahetu*). Vasubandhu says:
"Just as internal seeds produce the actual fruit, they are called producing causes (*janakahetu*)."
The remaining fruits that have already arisen are called the "projecting cause" (ākṣepa-hetu).
That which is the present seed producing the present body is called the "producing cause" (janma-hetu).
All things that produce the six sense bases and so forth are also termed "producing causes."
The "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) refers to things such as withered corpses and skeletal remains; although they have been reborn in other realms and so forth,
these remains still persist due to the power of their residual momentum (*saṃskāra-śakti*),
as will be explained below.
External seeds produce sprouts, stalks, and so forth as their generative causes;
these are the primary causes that produce withered grass and the like at the time of death.
This is the projecting cause (ākṣepa-hetu),
due to the power of its momentum;
however, when it reaches this stage, [it ceases].
Neither internal nor external seeds exist;
or else they have been born in another realm,
or the seeds have long since perished.
However, by the power of the momentum (*śakti*) from a previous birth, that [existence] is drawn forth and still persists;

thus, in this sense, the seed which is the cause of that birth is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*). Now, according to these two explanations, there is no distinct substantial entity for either the cause of birth or the projecting cause.
The two are spoken of because the one is viewed from the perspective of the distinct;
if there were no power of the drawing cause and its functional force,
all [consciousness] after death would suddenly cease, just like the birth-and-death of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If one were to encompass all four modes of birth and possess both causes,
the principle of being "without nature" (amūlaka) would be superior,
because in the transformation of birth and death there are no corpses.
However, according to the intention of Vasubandhu’s treatise,
the Great Master Asaṅga spoke of withered corpses and the like in order to establish the reason for citation;
thus he uttered this verse:
"Withering and death arise from being able to lead [others],
just as they cease spontaneously later.
Vasubandhu explains this, saying:
If there were no projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*),
there would be no fruit of withering and death, as if it were extinguished spontaneously at the end;
this is merely Vasubandhu’s abbreviated explanation.
The extensive commentary by Asvabhāva is also not contradictory;
although this [text] subsumes the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it does not conflict with it.

However, the fourth fascicle of the *Abhidharma* states that there are the "projectors" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*), as well as the "producers" (*abhinirvartaka*) and the "produced" (*abhinirvṛtta*).
The ninth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that both the projector and the projected are projecting causes (*ākṣepahetu*).
That which is capable of producing [a result] is called the productive cause (*janakahetu*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter ten, states:
"From ignorance up to sensation (*vedanā*), these are the projecting causes (*ākṣepahetu*)."

Craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of birth; this intention is to show that the seven factors prior to these, being as yet unmoistened, are called "projecting causes" because they project a distant result.
This is because they project a remote fruit.
It can moisten two factors as well as the existence that is moistened;
because it is proximate to the fruit, it is called the "cause of production," for it produces the fruit immediately.
This is also what is subsumed under "proximate" and "remote" herein.
Regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is based solely on the seeds that have already been moistened: the cause leading toward the fruit is considered proximate or remote.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, proximity and remoteness to the fruit are determined based on whether the state is one of being moistened or not yet moistened.
Nor is this contradictory. Next,
in the fourteenth [chapter], the "Analysis of Conditions," the internal and external seeds are distinguished as causes and non-causes,
and as being perfumed or unperfumed.
Treatise:
Internal seeds must necessarily arise from the nature of the causal condition of "arrival" (prāpti). Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Internal seeds are causal conditions;
they can produce results only through perfuming.
This is because, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), seeds must be nurtured and increased through perfuming before they can produce results.
Only that which has been newly perfumed and produced through perfuming can generate a fruit,
because it is a phenomenon belonging to sentient beings.
Treatise.
Regarding the statement, "The external seeds' perfuming continues until the produced fruit is distinguished," the commentary states:
The second fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:
Just as from charcoal, cow dung, and hair,
respectively, there arise large mustard seeds, blue lotus roots, and reeds;
it is not that the large mustard seeds and so forth are identical to the charcoal and so forth.
Arising and ceasing simultaneously while mutually perfuming one another,
it is born from that [perfuming];
this is called "unperfumed," such as the case of sesame seeds and flowers.
That which arises and perishes simultaneously with its cause, giving rise to fragrances and so forth through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*),
is called "possessing perfuming.
External seeds are not fixed in this regard.
Since internal seeds are fixed by perfuming, external seeds— being exclusively actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*)—
act as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to produce their resulting fruits.
Thus says the treatise.
This is because the internal seed must reach the point of producing its resultant fruit.
The commentary states:
This demonstrates that external seeds are not without causes and conditions.
Because they arise from internal seeds of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-bīja*),
as extensively analyzed in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* itself.
Below this, the second section explains the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a general inquiry;
second, a brief response.
This will be explained in detail later. Now, the treatise asks:
based on what meaning is the term "perfuming" (vāsanā) established?
The commentary states:
This marks the beginning of the initial inquiry.
[From] the Treatise:
Because that which is perfumed (*bhāvyamāna*) and that which perfumes (*bhāvaka*) reach [each other], it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
The commentary states:
this indicates the full meaning [of the term].
Explaining the term "perfuming" (vāsanā) as a brief answer to the question: "Perfuming" (vāsa) means to cause to arise, or alternatively, to lead to.
"Habituation" (abhyāsa) means...
Birth; proximity; number.
That is to say, it brings about the attainment of the fruit within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
causing the seeds to become proximate to arising and enabling them to grow.
This brief outline consists of three parts:
first, the four types of the perfumed;
second, the four types of the perfumer.
Third, because that which causes seeds to grow is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
Treatise:
What are the four characteristics of that which is perfumable?
The commentary states:
This is an extensive analysis.
Within it, there are three parts.
First, distinguishing the perfumable [basis] regarding the completeness or deficiency of its conditions;
second, distinguishing the perfuming agent regarding the completeness or deficiency of its conditions;
third, explaining the meaning of perfuming and so forth. Within the first [section], there are three parts.
First the question,
next the answer,
and finally the conclusion.
This is the first [point]. This same passage also appears in the second fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, though with slight differences;
these should be examined in their respective contexts. Now, as for the five categories of phenomena (*pañca-dharma-skandha*):
The first excludes material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and the mental factors (*caitta*) that accompany the seven consciousnesses;
the second excludes the virtuous phenomena of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhaphala*);
and the third excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Regarding the mental factors arising simultaneously:
the fourth [point] distinguishes the meaning of permitting perfuming (*vāsanā*) among different bodies occurring at the same time.
As for the absence [of such a distinction] in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, one should understand the differences by consulting each of the respective commentaries.
Treatise:
First, the nature of firm abiding... up to "this is that which is perfumed.
Commentary: [As follows].
This is the second answer.
From the beginningless beginning to the ultimate end.
The continuum of a certain type of nature that is uninterrupted and capable of sustaining habitual tendencies (vāsanā) is that which is perfumed (bhāvya).
Treatise.
"This [passage] excludes the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) because they are not objects of perfuming.
Commentary:
This excludes the seven evolving consciousnesses.
And those mental factors (caitta) [are included]; here, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) subsumes the mental factors.
Thus, the manas and so forth are all termed evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).
If it is admitted that they hold the seeds (bīja), [then they are the storehouse consciousness].
At the time of the untainted mind of the path of seeing on the first stage (*bhūmi*),
all contaminated seeds would have to be lost. Regarding "sound, wind,
and so forth," this refers to the exclusion of the forms included within the sense bases (*āyatana*) of the faculties, objects, and phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Those born in the formless realm lack physical form; thus,
they enter the meditative absorption of cessation and so forth.
Because the mind is also non-existent,
its nature is called "unstable.
Why, then, is it said here only of wind and sound?
This is because they are distinguished by being briefly and decisively excluded;
it does not mean that form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are not mentioned here,
nor that they are absent from this *Saṃgrahaṇī*.
If that which is stable can be perfumed,
then since the Buddha’s fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is stable,
it should be admitted that its nature as wholesome and so forth can also be perfumed.
This excludes the matter and mind of the Sautrāntika school from being perfumable,
because they do not abide stably.
Treatise.
"The two neutral natures... are that which is perfumed.
Commentary:
If a dharma is impartial and offers no resistance to the latencies of good or evil, [it is perfumable].
Only then can it receive perfuming,
because the indeterminate is not in opposition to the categories of the wholesome or the unwholesome.
Thus says the treatise.
This excludes both the wholesome and the defiled because they reach [their respective results]; therefore, they are not objects of perfuming (*bhāvya*).
The commentary states:
"It is like agarwood, musk, and so forth."
Furthermore, things such as garlic and leeks do not receive perfuming at all;
likewise, one who has abandoned their practice possesses a broad and tolerant nature and is thus able to accommodate circumstances,
whereas those who are clever but of an evil disposition cannot tolerate anything.
Furthermore, for example, the nature of goodness does not merely oppose non-goodness;
it also opposes itself.
This is because, like a heavy object that cannot retain the fragrance of sandalwood and the like, it is incapable of receiving them.
The same applies to the unwholesome and so forth;
therefore, they cannot be perfumed.
Furthermore, the indeterminate nature does not conflict with the wholesome or the unwholesome.
Just as the practitioner who has abandoned [defilements] does not contradict the facts, so too is the category of consciousness—such as that which is wholesome—precluded from being perfumed.
Within the seventh consciousness, it is likewise never the object of perfuming;
this is identical to the explanation provided later regarding its being exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Treatise:
For this reason, the Tathāgata does not newly undergo perfuming.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Because it is only through this neutral state that perfuming occurs,
the Tathāgata’s eighth untainted pure consciousness (anāsrava-vijñāna) exists solely within the causal stage as having been previously perfumed, carrying these ancient seeds.
It is not newly perfumed because it is exclusively wholesome; furthermore,
it contradicts [the nature of] the wholesome and so forth, being like aloeswood and other such substances.
This *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not distinguish [the seeds] as being identical to those in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, yet it describes them as "unperfumable.
What fault is there in perfuming at that time? It would contradict the nature of phenomena and involve [the fallacy of] addition or subtraction.
Because it is perfectly complete,
because there is a distinction between superior and inferior,
and because it cannot receive perfuming.
If it is of an indeterminate nature and is solely characterized by solidity,
then it is that which is perfumed.
The five mental factors, such as perception (saṃjñā), which arise simultaneously with the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), as well as space (ākāśa) and so forth,
should be the objects of perfuming (bhāvyam).
Treatise.
"Third, the nature of being perfumable... up to: 'this is that which is perfumed.
The commentary states:
If a dharma is sovereign and its essence is independent, not arising in reliance upon others..."
Its nature is not solid or dense; its substance is empty and porous, making it easily susceptible to perfuming.
Unlike stones and the like, it is capable of being perfumed.
Because it is not solid or dense and possesses porosity, it can accommodate seeds.
This is not the case, for it is firm and dense.
According to the treatise, because this [ālayavijñāna] obstructs the arrival of mental factors (caitta), it is not that which is perfumed (vāsya).
The commentary states:
The mental factors (caitta) that arise simultaneously with the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) number five;
their substance is not independent.
Because it arises dependently on others,
it is not that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*).
Although the sovereign mind (*citta*) must necessarily arise together with mental factors (*caitta*), [it is still not the locus of perfuming].
It does not refer to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
because it is designated as "king" in the sense of sovereignty.
This is not stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
What hindrance is there to [the ālayavijñāna] receiving perfuming?
This is explained in detail below in the section on "Contact and so forth are likewise."
It also excludes the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
because it is firm and dense;
like solid rock and the like, it does not receive perfuming (vāsanā).
Therefore, space and so forth cannot be perfumed. If that were the case, then adventitious dharmas such as arising upon consciousness should be capable of receiving perfuming;
however, these are now subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra*) and lack intrinsic reality of their own.
Because one speaks of the conventional based on the ultimate, it should further be said that [the self] would not be solid,
dense, substantial,
or sovereign.
Only then can it receive perfuming.
First, conditioned non-active phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are excluded;
next, provisional phenomena (prajñapti-dharma) are excluded.
Subsequently, mental factors (*caitta*) are excluded.

This excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), and mental factors, because they are dependent on others (*paratantra*) and lack stability or density; thus, they are not that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*).

This is not to say that [the ālayavijñāna] lacks a real substantial entity (*dravya-svabhāva*), for it was stated [previously] with the intention of explaining what will be discussed hereafter. Furthermore, the reason given here for its not having a real substantial entity is as follows: [it is because it lacks stability and density].

Since provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) do not exist prior [to their designation], what further need is there for exclusion? If that is so, how is it with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
If one says that true thusness (*tathatā*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), [then the same applies].
Terms such as "non-analytical" and so forth are merely conventional designations;
other conventional phenomena, such as "simultaneous arising," are not discussed here.
For this reason, it should be stated that [this state] is primarily wholesome.
Ignorance (avidyā) distinguishes [itself] from True Suchness (tathatā);
by this, one knows it is not that.
It also excludes [the influence of] perfuming upon the category of conventional consciousness and so forth.
If that which is susceptible to perfuming were itself the perfumed,
then perfuming should also be established as occurring across different bodies.
Treatise.
"Fourth, that which is capable of perfuming... up to: 'this is the perfumed.
The commentary states:
'The object' and 'that which is capable of harmonizing' constitute the meaning of association (*samprayoga*)."
If they exist at the same time and in the same location,
the entity that is perfumed is not identical to the perfuming agent,
nor is it entirely separate from it such as being on a consciousness within another body acting as the perfuming agent, and so forth.
Treatise:
This [consciousness] is not perfumable because it does not reach other bodies. Commentary:
[This means that]...
This excludes other bodies from being admitted as capable of being perfumed; furthermore,
because moments are not associated with one another across preceding and succeeding instants,
they lack the sense of conjunction and are therefore not objects of perfuming.
The masters of the Sautrāntika school argue that the consciousness of a preceding moment perfumes a subsequent moment of the same category. [The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] states:
"Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)... up to [the point where it is] not a mental factor (*caitta*), etc."
The commentary states:
This is the third conclusion.
Only the eighth consciousness possesses these four characteristics and can therefore serve as the perfumable (bhāvyam).
It is not the five mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously, nor are they the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*);
as for what is called the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*),
it is precisely [the basis] at the stage of being perfumed (*vāsana*).
If one says that the manifestation and the arising of the seeds occur at different times, how would one explain this?
Therefore, it is known that this very principle is correct. For those persons who lack the nature [of liberation], this seventh consciousness is fully endowed with these four characteristics.
Why is it not perfumed? Because the defiled and the neutral (avyākṛta) are incompatible with the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Now, when it is said that the neutral is exclusively the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), why among those things that can be perfumed is only that which is stable called "perfumable"? This is because [if it were otherwise], various material forms (rūpa) and so forth would arise even in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth, upon entering mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the like,
would lack any dharma to sustain their seeds;
[therefore,] if both were to sustain them...
This would result in the fallacy that a single entity produces two sprouts, as will be refuted later.
Why are wholesome states and the like unable to receive perfuming? Because they lack the capacity for containment, just like sandalwood and similar substances.

Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of spheres, it means that it is obtained whether the sphere is the sphere of the eye, the sphere of form, or any of the other spheres. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of elements, it means that it is obtained whether the element is the earth element, the water element, or any of the other elements. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of aggregates, it means that it is obtained whether the aggregate is the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, or any of the other aggregates. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of bases, it means that it is obtained whether the base is the base of the eye, the base of form, or any of the other bases. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of consciousnesses, it means that it is obtained whether the consciousness is visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, or any of the other consciousnesses. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of mental factors, it means that it is obtained whether the mental factor is associated with the five consciousnesses, associated with the mind-consciousness, or associated with the mental consciousness. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of conditions, it means that it is obtained whether the condition is the condition of cause, the condition of object, or any of the other conditions. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of fruits, it means that it is obtained whether the fruit is the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of dominance (*adhipatiphala*), or any of the other fruits. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of results, it means that it is obtained whether the result is the result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), the result of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*), or any of the other results. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of activities, it means that it is obtained whether the activity is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of intentions, it means that it is obtained whether the intention is directed toward the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, or the Formless Realm. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of aspirations, it means that it is obtained whether the aspiration is for the benefit of oneself, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of vows, it means that it is obtained whether the vow is the vow of a Disciple, the vow of a Solitary Buddha, or the vow of a Bodhisattva. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of dedications, it means that it is obtained whether the dedication is for the sake of worldly success, for the sake of liberation, or for the sake of omniscience. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of liberations, it means that it is obtained whether the liberation is the liberation of emptiness, the liberation of signlessness, or the liberation of wishlessness. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of concentrations, it means that it is obtained whether the concentration is the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, or the concentration of wishlessness. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of wisdoms, it means that it is obtained whether the wisdom is conventional wisdom, analytical wisdom, or ultimate wisdom. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of knowledges, it means that it is obtained whether the knowledge is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of subsequent realization (*anvayajñāna*), or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of insights, it means that it is obtained whether the insight is the insight of the Disciples, the insight of the Solitary Buddhas, or the insight of the Tathāgatas. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of paths, it means that it is obtained whether the path is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), or the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of fruits, it means that it is obtained whether the fruit is the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or any of the other fruits of the path. Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of nirvana, it means that it is obtained whether the nirvana is with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*), without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), or the nirvana of non-abiding (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*). Regarding the statement that it is obtained in all three types of dharmakāyas, it means that it is obtained whether the dharmakāya is the dharmakāya of the Śrāvakas, the dharmakāya of the Pratyekabuddhas, or the dharmakāya of the Tathāgatas. it is not produced from seeds that are truly functional causes and conditions.
That [uncontaminated object] serves merely as an object, and the uncontaminated [consciousness] is likewise; it does not necessarily have a functional utility.

Accordingly, this refers to the minds and mental factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, as well as the substance of the eighth consciousness and the fifth consciousness (the *manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with them.
Alternatively, regarding the objects of meditative concentration:
those that arise from actual seeds are all transformations of causes and conditions;
others, lacking practical efficacy, are merely nominal and resemble form, mind, and so forth.
The interpretation that "it transforms because it follows the power of conceptual differentiation" is correct;
it is free from all contradictions and difficulties.
Because the apprehending mind possesses spontaneous power,
the images transformed by it arise from actual seeds and are thus termed "transformation through causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*).
If the apprehending mind does not arise spontaneously, [the transformation is otherwise].
Although it arises spontaneously, it lacks superior power;
the transformed image is not produced from actual seeds and is thus called "discriminative transformation.
The former necessarily possesses utility.
There are no things that are useless;
for even those that appear later merely as objects according to one's disposition do not necessarily have a function.
However, if one discusses the dependent nature arising through the conditions of the provisional, it is indeed functional.
It is not like matter (*rūpa*), which possesses functions such as resistance;
rather, it is called "possessing function" because it accords with its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If the sixth retributive mind is associated with the five sensory consciousnesses, [it likewise possesses function].
It also transforms according to causes and conditions.

Its objects may be functional. Question: If, as previously stated, objects transform according to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then the objects transformed by meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*) and the five sensory consciousnesses would be entirely without function. Answer: Because they arise from seeds that correspond to their actual entities (*dravya*), the objects are functional.
For this reason, it is said that "it follows conceptualization. What is the meaning of this?
It means "following preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
"Conceptual transformation" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*) refers to the sense of various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) strongly deliberating and measuring.
In the concentrated mind and the five sensory consciousnesses,
although some arise through preparatory application (*prayoga*), they do not all involve forceful deliberation; therefore,
transformation necessarily has its function.
However, a single moment of mind can become two kinds.
For example, when a concentrated mind takes the eighteen realms as its object,
it conversely reveals that the eight [consciousnesses] all possess two transformations.
The objective realm of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-viṣaya) is subsumed under that which does not change according to the mind or its causal conditions.
Both the "solitary image" (kevala-pratibimba) and the "image with substance" (sadravya-pratibimba) are transformations of conceptualization (vikalpa).
Thus says the Treatise.
"The transformation of the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) must necessarily have real existence.

This demonstrates that the transformed forms and so forth arise from real seeds.

Treatise:
If it were the case that the mind and so forth, when undergoing transformation, could not serve as objects of cognition, [then they would lack these qualities].
The commentary states:
Since the objective aspects (nimittabhāga) of the mind and mental factors are like emanated minds (nirmāṇacitta) and so forth,
they do not take them as objects.
Conditions would then be useless.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states:
"All transformation-minds have no mind that is their own support; they have minds supported by others. The sixth fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, in this tenth [section], also says:
There is no mind that possesses a real entity as its own object of cognition;
rather, there is a mind that resembles an object of cognition through the appearance-part (nimittabhāga) manifested by the seeing-part (darśanabhāga),
like fire within a mirror.
...and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: If that is so, why do the mind and mental factors arise from the eighth [consciousness], given that they cannot undergo transformation and thus have no need to arise?
Treatise:
Its actual function must arise separately from this [cause].
Commentary states:
The seven consciousnesses and so forth must arise from the eighth consciousness in order to experience objects;
it is not the case that they fail to arise simply because they do not take [the eighth] as an object,
for even uncontaminated minds arise from it.
If there were an entity, the eighth consciousness would take it as its object;
since unconditioned phenomena possess an essence, they should be objects of the eighth consciousness.
Treatise:
Even the transformation into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would likewise lack practical utility.
[The commentary] states:
If the eighth consciousness were to take a truly existent unconditioned phenomenon as its object, [it would follow that it could not be transformed].
It is unconditioned yet without function, because it has not been realized;
if it resembles the unconditioned, it is not truly unconditioned.
Therefore, it is not subject to change.
Furthermore, the treatise uses the word "etc.
(ādi), and because the word "etc. also occurs within the category of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This also distinguishes the nominal dharmas (prajñapti-dharma) that are dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
Previously, the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) were answered;
now, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and the dissociated formations are explained.
There is no fault in this either.
This interpretation is the original one;
therefore, in the preceding question, it was asked: "Why is it that this consciousness cannot transform itself into something resembling mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta), etc.?"
Since it is stated that [the objects] are "equal," one takes as [objects] both provisional phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
Therefore, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) does not take mind and mental factors as its objects.
The commentary states:
This is the summary. Question: If the causal conditions for tainted consciousness consist of appearances, it need not be the case that the appearances of conceptualization exist substantially.
Since there is no conceptual differentiation in the untainted state,
it should not take non-existence as its object;
and since all things arise from causes and conditions, they should all take reality as their object.

Treatise: Upon reaching the stage of the untainted (anāsrava), one also manifests their reflection. Commentary: * **Treatise:** "Upon reaching the stage of the untainted, one also manifests their reflection. * **Commentary:** This explains that when one attains the state of the untainted, the images of those [objects] likewise appear as reflections.
In the untainted state, it is associated with superior wisdom;
although there is no conceptualization that involves deliberation or grasping at signs,
it is nevertheless limpid and pure.
It is not as with contaminated phenomena, whose essence is turbid;
even if they are currently of no use, they still manifest their reflections.
Thus, the object of non-existence and the reflections of the mind and so forth serve as the basis for those reflections and the like.
Because it is personally realized,
one knows that there is no "is" and no "is not," and thus conditions upon non-existence and so forth.
Treatise.
If it were not so, the Buddhas would not be omniscient.
The commentary states:
Because they do not know non-existence, they would not be omniscient.
Because the Buddha’s eighth consciousness manifests the reflections of all phenomena, it is called "omniscience" (*sarvajñā*);
this is because it is a universal cognition.
If that is so, then what of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of all Buddhas?
It should also take its own associated mental factors as objects;
since these constitute universal knowledge (*sarvajñāna*), there is no fault in admitting this.
At the beginning of the fascicle, it was merely refuting the view that the Sthavira Dharmamitra alone acts as the object.

Because it does not exclude the remote [object]. If that were so, it would follow that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) would have different objects of cognition (*ālambana*), because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of its own nature does not take itself as an object. This is also not the case.
Since the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) and the other seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) share the same object, there is no fault.
Furthermore, it is explained that even though the associated mental factors (*caitta*) do not mutually perceive one another, there is likewise no fault.
Because self-cognition establishes the universal knowledge through its objective aspect;
because the subjective aspect apprehends the associated mind;
and because all phenomena are thus exhausted.
Since self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) can also take the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) as its object,
there is no fault in not mentioning self-cognition when speaking merely of the seeing-parts having the same object of cognition (ālambana).
What error would there be in this?
Treatise:
Therefore, there are both the actual states of outflow and the seeds of outflow. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Because this eighth consciousness cannot fully take all eighteen realms as its objects,
it differs between the contaminated state and the uncontaminated state; thus,
there is a distinction in the breadth or narrowness and the superiority or inferiority of their respective objects.
Regarding the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, they do not necessarily have a function.
It should be analyzed that it is only the two means of valid cognition— direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)— that possess a function.
Treatise:
[The seeds] in the desire and form realms reach to and take as objects impure (sāsrava) seeds.
Commentary states:
Third, the distinctions between the realms of the three worlds are clarified.
According to those such as Pūrṇavardhana, the physical environment and bodies are also transformed within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
In this regard, there is only the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla.
This summarizes the preceding discussion on the objects of the three realms.
The treatise states:
Because of weariness with form, one takes this form as an object.
The commentary states:
"Formless and formless" means that because one has become weary of and detached from form.
Because there is no fruit of karma.
If it were the case that one could also take the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration as an object,
this has already been explained previously.
This is not contrary to principle.
Within this very text, it is stated that if [the powers] consist of concentration and supernormal power (*samādhi-abhijñā*),
they take as their object all places— whether within the same realm and the same stage, or across different realms and different stages.
The fifty-third [fascicle] states:
"Because one attains mastery over all forms within the formless realm concentrations.
This concludes the second section, the explanation of the "unknowable" (*anabhijñeya*).
There are two parts:
first, an explanation of what is unknowable;
second, a discussion consisting of questions and answers.
Treatise:
That which is "unknowable" is extremely difficult to comprehend.
Commentary: [As stated above].
Regarding the statement "it is unknowable" in the preceding verse:
the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the first, the division of views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), is difficult to discern.
[End of] Treatise.
Alternatively, it may be that the object of this [consciousness] reaches a state called "unknowable.
The commentary states:
herein, the second aspect, the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective part), is difficult to know.
The internal appropriated objects consist of the contaminated seeds and the embodied organism with its sense faculties, both of which are subtle and difficult to know;
the external non-appropriated world-receptacle is difficult to know because of its vast magnitude.
This concludes the second section.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51:
"In the desire realm, one takes a narrow and small object as a condition. Here, "small" refers to the body and the environment (*bhājanaloka*).
The form realm is vast;
this is also in terms of the bodies and the physical world (bhājanaloka),
because the first dhyāna is equal in scale to a small chiliocosm.
The magnitude of the body can be known.
In the spheres of Infinite Space and Infinite Consciousness, one takes as objects the immeasurable appropriated realms;
this refers specifically to the time when seeds give rise to manifesting consciousnesses.
Because one forms this mode of practice and understanding,
the seeds of these immeasurable modes of practice and understanding are called "the objects of appropriation based on the immeasurable."

The spheres of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth should be understood accordingly. Since it takes as its object the specific functional capacities (*śakti-viśeṣa*) upon the seeds, one might conclude that it also takes the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) as its objects; however, this reasoning is incorrect.
What is called "condition" (ālambana) is designated from the perspective of the fruit.
It does not mean that this seed conditions immeasurable modes of understanding;
therefore, it does not condition mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the like.
As previously stated,
the treatise asks:
Why is it that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of consciousness is difficult to know?
The commentary states:
This refers to external inquiries,
such as those from the Sautrāntikas and the Sarvāstivādins.
Since that which has already passed is difficult to know, it should not be consciousness;
this mention of "aspects" (ākāra) refers merely to the seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga).
[End of] Treatise.
"Just as [the attainment] must be believed to exist within the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Commentary states:
This is an answer by means of an analogy.
This answers the Sautrāntika school.
Since they ultimately maintain that the mind exists during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
this response is given by way of analogy.

Just as in the meditative attainment of cessation there is a consciousness that does not depart from the body, so too is [the continuity of] activity difficult to discern; one should therefore believe that the eighth consciousness exists as a constant essence.
This answers both the Sthavira and the later Sautrāntikas.
There is a subtle mental consciousness;
this may be so in this case.
However, according to the Sarvāstivādins and others, there is no consciousness during meditative absorption.
It is like a tertian malaria.
[This is] the answer from the Sarvāstivāda,
because they do not admit that consciousness exists within the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Answer this with reason.
Treatise:
However, one must necessarily admit that it is just as when there is a mind.
The commentary states:
Inference is as explained in the text. Thus concludes the treatise.
It should be understood that the same applies to states such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
The commentary states:
"In this case as well, the thesis to be established is the same."

The two schools’ respective tenets differ in their interpretations, yet there is no fault of indefiniteness (anaikāntika). Within this context, there are also states such as unconsciousness, fainting, and sleep;
these are accepted only by [the opponent], or they are all equal [in being states] wherein consciousness exists.
